TAQ1.brief: A view mode changes how the viewport draws your level. The normal mode is called Lit, but other modes show only one part of the picture, such as the lighting alone or how much work each surface costs the graphics card. Technical artists use these modes to understand what the engine is doing and to find problems. In this quest you look at the same camera view in several view modes and compare them.
checklist: Open any level that has a few meshes, lights and materials in it. A template level is fine.
Pick one camera view and keep it for the whole quest. Take a screenshot of it in the Lit, Unlit and Wireframe view modes.
Switch to the Detail Lighting view mode, and then to Lighting Only. Look at what changes on surfaces that use normal maps, which are textures that add small surface detail.
Switch to the Shader Complexity view mode, which colors each surface by how expensive its material is to draw. Find the most expensive color on the screen and note which object it is.
Switch to the Light Complexity view mode. Note which surface is affected by the most lights.
When you are done, switch the viewport back to Lit.
TAQ1.done_when: Send one image that shows 6 labeled views from the same camera (Lit, Unlit, Wireframe, Detail Lighting, Shader Complexity and Light Complexity). Add one line about the most expensive object you found.

TAQ2.brief: Frames per second (fps) tells you how smoothly the game runs, but it does not tell you why it is slow. The console command stat unit splits the time of one frame into parts: the game logic, the rendering thread (called Draw) and the graphics card (GPU). The part that takes the longest is called the bottleneck, and it shows you where to look. In this quest you read these numbers, make the level heavier on purpose, and read them again.
checklist: Open a level and start Play In Editor (PIE), which runs the game inside the editor.
Press the ~ key to open the console, the line where you can type commands. Type stat fps and press Enter, then type stat unit and press Enter.
Write down the Frame, Game, Draw (rendering thread) and GPU times. They are shown in milliseconds.
Stop PIE. Add something heavy to the level, for example 20 movable point lights close together, or many translucent planes.
Start PIE again with stat unit turned on. Write down the new numbers.
Compare the two sets of numbers and see which time grew the most. That time shows where your bottleneck is.
TAQ2.done_when: Send two screenshots with stat unit visible, one from before and one from after you added the heavy objects. Add two lines: one that says which time grew the most, and one that says what you think caused it.

TAQ3.brief: A naming convention is a set of rules for how you name your assets. A common rule is to start each name with a short prefix that shows the type, such as SM_ for a Static Mesh or T_ for a texture. Clear names help you, your team and your tools find assets fast. In this quest you build a tidy folder structure, rename some assets with prefixes, and write a short naming rule of your own.
checklist: In the Content Browser, make a folder named TechArt. Inside it, make the sub-folders Meshes, Materials, Textures, FX and Tools.
Move or create at least 6 assets in these folders. Use a mix of meshes, materials, material instances and textures.
Rename each asset in the form Prefix_AssetName_Descriptor. For example: SM_Crate, M_Crate, MI_Crate_Red, T_Crate_BaseColor and T_Crate_Normal.

After you have moved things, right-click the TechArt folder and choose Fix Up Redirectors. Redirectors are small leftover files that point from the old location of an asset to the new one, and this command cleans them up.
Type T_ in the search box of the Content Browser. Check that only textures show up.
Write a short naming rule of 5 lines for your own project and save it in a text file.
TAQ3.done_when: Send a screenshot of the TechArt folder tree with the renamed assets visible, and add your 5-line naming rule.

TAQ4.brief: The Construction Script is a graph inside a Blueprint that runs in the editor each time you place the Blueprint or change one of its settings. You can use it to make a Blueprint build itself, so you do not have to place every piece by hand. In this quest you make a fence Blueprint that creates a row of meshes from two numbers: how many posts there are and how far apart they stand.
checklist: Create an Actor Blueprint named BP_FenceRow. Add an Instanced Static Mesh component, which draws many copies of one mesh in a cheap way, and give it a simple mesh such as a cube or a fence post.

Add a variable named Count of type Integer and a variable named Spacing of type Float. Click the eye icon next to each one so that it is open. This makes both variables Instance Editable, which means you can change them on each copy in the level.
Open the Construction Script. First call Clear Instances on the component, and then add a For Loop that goes from 0 to Count - 1.
Inside the loop, call Add Instance. Give it a relative location where X is Index * Spacing, so each new copy is placed a little further along.
Place BP_FenceRow in the level. Change Count and Spacing in the Details panel and watch the fence rebuild itself.
Place a second copy of BP_FenceRow and give it different values.
TAQ4.done_when: Send a screenshot that shows two BP_FenceRow copies with different Count values and the Details panel visible. Also send a screenshot of the Construction Script graph.

TAQ5.brief: Niagara is the system Unreal uses to make visual effects such as fire, smoke, sparks and magic. An effect is saved as a Niagara System, and inside it are one or more emitters, which are the parts that create the particles. Each emitter is built from small blocks called modules that you can change. In this quest you create a system from a template, change how many particles it makes, how long they live and what color they have, and place it in a level.
checklist: Right-click in the Content Browser and choose FX, then Niagara System. Pick a template that spawns particles all the time, such as Fountain.
Name the new asset FXS_TestFountain. Double-click it to open it in the Niagara Editor.
Find the Spawn Rate module in the Emitter Update group. Change the rate, which is the number of new particles each second, and watch the preview.
In the Particle Spawn group, open the Initialize Particle module. Set Lifetime Mode to Random and enter a Minimum and a Maximum, so each particle lives for a different time.
Change the particle Color in the Initialize Particle module.
Drag FXS_TestFountain from the Content Browser into your level, and check that it looks right there.
TAQ5.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Niagara Editor with the emitter stack open, so that Spawn Rate and Initialize Particle are visible. Also send one screenshot of the effect in the level.

TAQ6.brief: Python is a programming language that the Unreal editor can run. With a short Python script you can automate boring editor work, such as checking or renaming many assets, that you would otherwise do by hand. In this quest you turn on Python in the editor, run two lines in the Python console, and then save the code as a script file and run it.
checklist: Open Edit > Plugins and look in the Scripting category. Enable the Python Editor Script Plugin and Editor Scripting Utilities, and then restart the editor.
Open the Output Log. Next to the input line at the bottom, switch the input from Cmd to Python. Then type this line and press Enter: unreal.log("Hello from Python")
Select 3 or more assets in the Content Browser.
In the Python console, type this line and press Enter: print([a.get_name() for a in unreal.EditorUtilityLibrary.get_selected_assets()])
Save the same code in a file named list_selected.py inside the Content/Python folder of your project. Add the line import unreal at the top of the file.
Run the file with File > Execute Python Script, and check the result in the Output Log.
TAQ6.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Output Log that shows your Hello line and the list of selected asset names. Also add the text of list_selected.py.

TAQ7.brief: An Editor Utility Blueprint is a Blueprint that runs in the editor and not in the game. When its parent class is AssetActionUtility, its functions appear in the right-click menu of the Content Browser, and they work on all the assets you have selected. This can turn a long manual task into one click. In this quest you build a right-click action that adds a prefix to the names of many assets at once.
checklist: In your TechArt/Tools folder, right-click and choose Editor Utilities, then Editor Utility Blueprint. Pick AssetActionUtility as the parent class, and name the new asset EUB_AssetActions.
Open it and add a function named AddPrefix. Give the function a String input called Prefix.
Inside the function, add Get Selected Assets and connect it to a For Each Loop. In the loop, call Rename Asset, and make the new name from Prefix followed by the old object name.
Click Compile and then Save. Make a few test assets that have no prefix in their names.
Select the test assets in the Content Browser and right-click them. Run your action from the Scripted Asset Actions menu.
Add a check to the function so the action skips assets whose names already start with the prefix.
TAQ7.done_when: Send a screenshot of the right-click menu that shows your action, a before and after screenshot of the renamed assets, and a screenshot of the function graph.

TAQ8.brief: Textures are the images that materials use, and they take up a large part of a game's memory. A few settings on each texture decide how good it looks and how much memory it costs. One of them is sRGB, which should be on for color images and off for images that store data. In this quest you import three textures for one asset and give each one the correct settings.
checklist: Import three textures for one asset: a color map named T_Crate_BaseColor, a normal map named T_Crate_Normal, and a packed mask named T_Crate_ORM. A packed mask stores a different grayscale image in each color channel.
Double-click each texture to open it in the Texture Editor. Keep sRGB turned on for the color map, and turn sRGB off for the mask.
Set Compression Settings on two of them: choose Normalmap for the normal map and Masks for the mask texture.
Set a Texture Group for each texture, for example World and WorldNormalMap.
Note the Resource Size of each texture, which is how much memory it uses. Then set LOD Bias to 1 on one texture and note its new size.

Import one more texture whose size is not a power of two (powers of two are sizes such as 512 or 1024). Check how many mips it has. Mips are the smaller copies of a texture that are used when it is far away.
TAQ8.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Details panel for T_Crate_ORM with sRGB off and the Masks compression visible. Also add a short table of the 3 textures that lists size, sRGB, compression and Resource Size for each.

TAQ9.brief: A test bed is a small level that you build only for testing. It gives you one known place where you can check materials, effects and tools, and you can use it again in later quests. In this quest you build a lit test room and bring together what you made so far: your self-building prop, a Niagara effect, your named folders and your right-click action.
checklist: Build a small room in a level named L_TA_TestBed. It needs a floor, walls, one directional light and at least two point lights.
Put a notes board in the room, made from a text render or a textured plane. On it, list the view modes and stat commands you use to check the room.
Place your construction-script prop (BP_FenceRow or a similar one) in the room with at least two different settings.
Place one Niagara system in the room. Its name should start with FXS_.
Keep all the assets in a TechArt folder and give them the correct prefixes. Use your Scripted Action (EUB_AssetActions) on them at least once.
Check the room in the Lit view mode, in the Shader Complexity view mode, and with stat unit. Write down the numbers you see.
Write 5 lines that say what the room tests, what the most expensive thing in it is, and one fix you would try.
TAQ9.done_when: Send screenshots of the room in Lit and in Shader Complexity, one screenshot with stat unit visible, a screenshot of the Content Browser folder, and your 5-line writeup. A mentor reviews it.

TAQ10.brief: LOD means Level of Detail. A mesh can have several versions with fewer and fewer triangles, and Unreal shows a simpler version when the object is far from the camera. This saves work for the graphics card, because far-away objects do not need all their triangles. In this quest you let Unreal create LODs for a mesh in two ways, with a preset group and by hand, and you watch them switch in the level.
checklist: Duplicate a mesh, for example SM_Rock from the Starter Content, and name the copy SM_Rock_LODTest.
Double-click it to open it in the Static Mesh Editor. In the LOD Settings section, set LOD Group to SmallProp and accept the change when the editor asks.
Check that Auto Compute LOD Distances is turned on. Note the triangle count of each LOD.
Make a second copy of the mesh and set it up by hand. Set Number of LODs to 4, and then set Percent Triangles to 75, 25 and 12 for LOD1, LOD2 and LOD3.
Place both meshes in a level. Turn on the LOD Coloration view mode, which gives each LOD its own color, and move the camera away slowly.
TAQ10.done_when: Send a screenshot of the LOD Settings that shows the triangle count of each LOD. Also send one screenshot in the LOD Coloration view mode with at least two LOD colors visible.

TAQ11.brief: A Material Parameter Collection (MPC) is an asset that holds a list of named values. Any material can read these values, so when you change one value, every material that uses it changes at the same moment. This is how one number can control the look of a whole level, such as weather, time of day or damage. In this quest you make a collection with a Wetness value and a tint color, use it in two materials, and change it from a Blueprint while the game runs.
checklist: In the Content Browser, right-click, choose Material, and then click Material Parameter Collection. Name the new asset MPC_World.
Open MPC_World. Add a Scalar Parameter (a single number) named Wetness with a default of 0, and a Vector Parameter (a color) named WorldTint with a default of white.

Open two different materials, for example M_Rock and M_Ground. In each one, add a Collection Parameter node set to MPC_World. Use Wetness to darken Base Color and to lower Roughness, and multiply Base Color by WorldTint.
Place meshes that use both materials, or instances of them, in a test level. Change Wetness in MPC_World and watch every mesh update at once.

Make a Blueprint named BP_WeatherControl. On Begin Play, use a Timeline that goes from 0 to 1 over 5 seconds to drive a Set Scalar Parameter Value node. On that node, set Collection to MPC_World and Parameter to Wetness.
Add a key press event that calls Set Vector Parameter Value to change WorldTint to a warm evening color.
Start Play in Editor and test both parts: first the world gets wet, and then the tint changes when you press the key.
TAQ11.done_when: Send two screenshots from PIE, one dry and one wet with the new tint. Also send one screenshot of the BP_WeatherControl graph that shows the Set Scalar Parameter Value node with MPC_World selected.

TAQ12.brief: A User parameter is a value on a Niagara system that can be set from outside the effect, for example from a Blueprint. With User parameters, one effect can react to what happens in the game, and you do not need to make a new copy of the effect for each case. In this quest you add two User parameters to a fountain effect, one for the spawn rate and one for the color, and you change them with a key press while the game runs.
checklist: Make a Niagara system named NS_Fountain from a simple emitter template. For example, use Fountain, or Simple Sprite Burst with a Spawn Rate module added.
In the Parameters panel, add a User parameter of type float named SpawnRate, and a User parameter of type Linear Color named TintColor.
Link the Spawn Rate module to User SpawnRate, and link the particle Color to User TintColor. Give both parameters sensible default values.
Place NS_Fountain in a level. Select it and check that both values show in the Details panel under Override Parameters.

Make a Blueprint named BP_FountainController that has a Niagara component, or a reference to the system you placed. On a key press, call Set Niagara Variable (Float) for SpawnRate and Set Niagara Variable (LinearColor) for TintColor.
Start Play in Editor and press the key. Confirm that the effect changes its rate and color, and that you did not have to edit the Niagara asset.
TAQ12.done_when: Send two PIE screenshots, one from before the key press and one from after. Also send one screenshot of the Blueprint graph with the Set Niagara Variable nodes.
